title: Independence from Britain Under Seewoosagur Ramgoolam
description: On March 12, 1968, Mauritius became independent within the Commonwealth after a narrow referendum-like 1967 election victory by the Independence Party led by Sir Seewoosagur Ramgoolam. The Indo-Mauritian-led coalition prevailed over the PMSD's Franco-Creole bloc that had favored continued association with Britain, setting the country on a parliamentary democratic path with Queen Elizabeth II as head of state.

title: Port Louis Communal Riots Between Creoles and Muslims
description: In the weeks surrounding independence, intense communal rioting between Creole and Muslim communities in Port Louis killed at least 25 people and forced thousands to flee. British troops were deployed under a state of emergency to restore order, exposing deep ethnic tensions in the new multi-ethnic state and shaping early constitutional safeguards for minorities.

title: Chagos Archipelago Excised to Form British Indian Ocean Territory
description: Britain detached the Chagos Archipelago from Mauritius in 1965 to create the British Indian Ocean Territory and continued the policy after independence in 1968, retaining the islands for a US military base on Diego Garcia. Mauritius accepted a £3 million payment under duress but never recognised the excision as lawful, planting the seed for a half-century sovereignty dispute.

title: Founding of Mouvement Militant Mauricien (MMM)
description: Paul Berenger and other young radicals founded the Mouvement Militant Mauricien, a left-wing trade-union-rooted party promising to break the communal mould of Mauritian politics with class-based mobilisation. The MMM rapidly built support across ethnic lines, especially among Creole and younger Indo-Mauritian workers, becoming the main challenger to Ramgoolam's Labour Party.

title: State of Emergency and Mass Arrests of MMM Leaders
description: Following dock strikes and rising MMM popularity, Ramgoolam's government imposed a state of emergency in December 1971, postponed elections by four years, and detained Paul Berenger and other MMM leaders without trial. Press censorship was tightened and political activity restricted, marking the most authoritarian episode of independent Mauritian politics.

title: Sugar Boom Funds Welfare State Expansion
description: World sugar prices surged in 1973-74, generating windfall revenues that the Ramgoolam government channelled into free secondary education, expanded health care, and old-age pensions. The boom funded the welfare-state foundations that would underpin Mauritian human-development gains, even as it deepened dependence on a single commodity.

title: First Post-Emergency Election: Hung Parliament
description: December 1976 elections produced a hung parliament with the MMM emerging as the largest single party but Ramgoolam's Labour-PMSD coalition forming the government. The vote ended the state of emergency in practice and showed the MMM's cross-communal appeal, though Berenger remained excluded from power.

title: Sugar Price Crash Triggers Balance-of-Payments Crisis
description: Collapsing world sugar prices and second-oil-shock import costs pushed Mauritius into a severe balance-of-payments crisis in 1979, exhausting foreign reserves and forcing emergency measures. The crisis exposed the danger of monocrop dependence and prompted the government to seek IMF assistance.

title: First IMF Standby and Structural Adjustment Begins
description: Mauritius signed its first IMF standby agreement in 1979 and entered four years of austerity including currency devaluation, subsidy cuts, and wage restraint. The adjustment programme was painful socially but credited with stabilising public finances and clearing the way for the export-led pivot of the mid-1980s.

title: Cyclone Claudette Devastates Sugar Crop
description: Tropical Cyclone Claudette struck Mauritius in December 1979 and was followed by further storms in 1980, destroying a large share of the sugar harvest and worsening the foreign-exchange crisis. The disasters reinforced arguments for economic diversification away from cyclone-vulnerable monoculture.

title: MMM-PSM '60-0' Landslide Sweeps Travaillons Generation to Power
description: In June 1982 the MMM-PSM alliance under Aneerood Jugnauth as Prime Minister and Paul Berenger as Finance Minister won every elected seat, ending the Ramgoolam era. The 'Travaillons' ('Let Us Work') campaign promised socialist transformation, but the new government rapidly moderated under IMF pressure and would split within nine months.

title: MMM-PSM Coalition Collapses; Jugnauth Founds MSM
description: Ideological and personal rifts split the MMM-PSM coalition in March 1983, with Jugnauth breaking away to form the Mouvement Socialiste Mauricien (MSM) and forming a new alliance with Labour and PMSD. The August 1983 snap election confirmed the realignment, entrenching a fluid coalition politics that would define Mauritius for the next four decades.

title: Export Processing Zone Takes Off — Textile Boom Begins
description: The Export Processing Zone framework, in place since 1970 but underused, surged in the mid-1980s as Hong Kong investors and local firms exploited preferential textile access to Europe under the Multi-Fibre Arrangement and the Lome Convention. EPZ employment leapt from under 20,000 to over 80,000 by the late 1980s, transforming Mauritius from sugar-island to manufacturing exporter.

title: Air Mauritius Heroin Trafficking Scandal
description: Four MSM party officials, including a member of parliament, were arrested in Amsterdam in December 1985 with heroin in their luggage on an Air Mauritius flight. The scandal exposed political-criminal networks at the heart of the ruling party and became a defining corruption episode of the Jugnauth era, though convictions were limited and political consequences contained.

title: Economic Take-Off — GDP Growth Above 6 Percent
description: By 1987 Mauritius was recording sustained GDP growth above 6 percent on the back of EPZ exports, tourism, and revived sugar prices, with unemployment falling sharply from a 1983 peak above 20 percent. The 'Mauritian miracle' narrative began to crystallise in development economics literature as a counter-example to African stagnation.

title: Stock Exchange of Mauritius Established
description: The Stock Exchange of Mauritius opened in July 1988 as part of a broader financial-sector liberalisation, providing a domestic capital market for listed companies and signalling the government's intent to develop financial services. The exchange grew slowly but laid groundwork for the offshore-finance pivot of the 1990s.

title: Jugnauth-MMM Alliance Wins Snap Election on Republic Pledge
description: Jugnauth's MSM-MMM-Labour alliance won the September 1991 election with a manifesto pledge to transform Mauritius into a republic within the Commonwealth. The result gave Jugnauth a mandate to push the constitutional change through parliament against PMSD opposition.

title: Mauritius Becomes a Republic; Cassam Uteem First President
description: On March 12, 1992, the 24th anniversary of independence, Mauritius became a republic within the Commonwealth, replacing the Queen with a ceremonial president elected by parliament. Cassam Uteem, the first Muslim head of state, was elected as first President, while executive power remained with the Prime Minister.

title: Offshore Financial Sector Launched
description: Parliament passed the Mauritius Offshore Business Activities Act and related legislation in 1992, creating the regulatory framework for an offshore financial centre with low tax rates and double-taxation treaties, especially with India. The sector grew rapidly through the 1990s, becoming a major source of fee income but also drawing later allegations of tax-haven facilitation.

title: Cyclone Hollanda Causes Widespread Damage
description: Tropical Cyclone Hollanda struck Mauritius on February 10, 1994 with winds above 200 km/h, killing two people, injuring more than a thousand, and destroying or damaging tens of thousands of homes. Damage was estimated at around US$135 million and the storm became the benchmark cyclone event of the 1990s for Mauritian disaster planning.

title: Labour-MMM Landslide Ousts Jugnauth After 13 Years
description: Navin Ramgoolam's Labour Party in alliance with the MMM swept the December 1995 election by a 60-0 elected-seat margin, ending Jugnauth's 13-year tenure. Ramgoolam, son of independence leader Seewoosagur Ramgoolam, became Prime Minister with Berenger as deputy in a coalition that would itself fracture within two years.

title: MMM Walks Out of Government; Labour Continues Alone
description: Tensions over portfolios and policy direction led the MMM to withdraw from the Labour-MMM coalition in June 1997, leaving Ramgoolam to govern with a slim majority and Berenger to return to opposition. The split set up the rotation politics that characterised the next two decades.

title: Kaya Riots — Communal Violence After Singer's Death in Custody
description: Seggae musician Kaya (Joseph Reginald Topize) died in police custody on February 21, 1999, triggering days of rioting led primarily by Creole youth in Port Louis, Roche Bois, and other townships. At least four people were killed, the riots exposed long-suppressed Creole grievances about marginalisation by the Indo-Mauritian-dominated state, and the episode became a turning point in national debates about ethnic inequality.

title: MSM-MMM Alliance Wins Election; Jugnauth-Berenger Power-Sharing Deal
description: The September 2000 election produced a 54-6 victory for the MSM-MMM alliance, returning Aneerood Jugnauth as Prime Minister with an unprecedented agreement to hand power to Paul Berenger after three years. The deal made Berenger the first non-Hindu Prime Minister of Mauritius when it was honored in 2003.

title: ICT Sector Strategy and Cybercity Initiative Launched
description: The government launched the 'Cybercity' initiative at Ebene with state-led infrastructure investment to diversify into ICT, business-process outsourcing and back-office services. The strategy attracted Indian IT firms and laid the foundation for ICT to become a major contributor to GDP by the 2010s.

title: Berenger Becomes Prime Minister — First Non-Hindu Head of Government
description: Honoring the 2000 power-sharing agreement, Aneerood Jugnauth resigned as Prime Minister to become President in September 2003, and Paul Berenger took office as Prime Minister — the first Franco-Mauritian and first non-Hindu to hold the post. The transition was widely praised internationally as a demonstration of mature democratic alternation.

title: Navin Ramgoolam Returns to Power in Alliance Sociale Sweep
description: The July 2005 election delivered a 38-22 victory for Navin Ramgoolam's Alliance Sociale (Labour-PMXD-MR-Verts) over the MSM-MMM, returning Ramgoolam to the prime ministership. The campaign focused on economic anxieties as the EU sugar-protocol reforms and the end of the Multi-Fibre Arrangement threatened the two pillars of Mauritian export economy.

title: Sugar Protocol Ends — EU Phases Out Preferential Prices
description: The EU-ACP Sugar Protocol began phased dismantling in 2006, ending forty years of guaranteed-above-market prices for Mauritian sugar exports to Europe. Mauritius secured transitional accompanying measures funding to restructure the industry through mechanisation, diversification into specialty sugars and ethanol, and consolidation of mills.

title: Multi-Fibre Arrangement Ends — Textile Sector Crisis
description: The end of the Multi-Fibre Arrangement quotas in 2005 and full WTO textile liberalisation by 2006 triggered the closure of dozens of EPZ factories and the loss of more than 25,000 textile jobs over several years as Asian competition intensified. The crisis accelerated diversification into higher-value services and tourism.

title: Business Facilitation Act and 'Doing Business' Reforms
description: Parliament passed the Business Facilitation Act in 2006, slashing the time and cost of starting a business and consolidating regulatory approvals into a one-stop framework. The reforms drove Mauritius up the World Bank Doing Business rankings to first in Africa, anchoring its post-MFA reinvention as a services hub.

title: Tax Reform — Flat 15 Percent Personal and Corporate Income Tax
description: Finance Minister Rama Sithanen's 2006-07 budget introduced a 15 percent flat rate for both personal and corporate income tax, replacing the previous progressive system. The reform was controversial for its distributional effects but credited with broadening the tax base and reinforcing Mauritius's competitiveness as a financial-services hub.

title: Resilient Performance Through Global Financial Crisis
description: Despite a sharp drop in tourism arrivals from Europe and falling textile and sugar exports, Mauritius weathered the 2008-09 global financial crisis without recession, recording positive growth and avoiding bank failures. The performance was credited to prudent macroeconomic management, fiscal stimulus, and the diversification achieved over the previous decade.

title: Ramgoolam Re-elected with Alliance de l'Avenir
description: Navin Ramgoolam's Alliance de l'Avenir (Labour-PMSD-MSM) won the May 2010 election by 41-18 over the MMM, returning him for a second consecutive term. The result reinforced Labour's dominance of post-crisis politics and Ramgoolam's central place in the system.

title: MedPoint Clinic Affair — Corruption Allegations Against Jugnauth Family
description: The state's purchase of the MedPoint clinic from a company linked to Pravind Jugnauth's family in late 2010 triggered a corruption case that would dog Mauritian politics for years. Pravind Jugnauth was convicted by a magistrate in 2015, the conviction was overturned by the Supreme Court in 2016, and the Privy Council ultimately acquitted him in 2019.

title: MSM Walks Out of Government Over MedPoint Investigation
description: Pravind Jugnauth and the MSM withdrew from the Ramgoolam government in mid-2012 amid the deepening MedPoint controversy, ending a fragile coalition and forcing Labour to govern with reduced parliamentary support. The split realigned coalition politics ahead of 2014.

title: India-Mauritius Tax Treaty Renegotiation Talks Intensify
description: India intensified pressure to renegotiate the 1983 India-Mauritius double-taxation treaty that had channelled an estimated 30 percent of foreign direct investment into India through Mauritian holding structures. The dispute exposed the offshore-finance sector's reliance on a single bilateral arrangement and prompted Mauritian diversification efforts toward Africa.

title: MSM-PMSD-ML Lepep Alliance Sweeps Election; Jugnauth Returns
description: In a stunning December 2014 result, Aneerood Jugnauth's MSM-PMSD-ML 'Lepep' alliance won 47 of 60 elected seats against Ramgoolam's Labour-MMM 'Unity' alliance, which captured only 13. Ramgoolam himself lost his seat, and Jugnauth, then 84, returned for a fourth term as Prime Minister on a platform of fighting corruption.

title: Navin Ramgoolam Arrested in Safe-Box Cash Scandal
description: Police searching Navin Ramgoolam's home in February 2015 reportedly found 220 million rupees (about US$6 million) in cash in safes, leading to his arrest on money-laundering charges. The case became a defining corruption controversy of the post-2014 political order, though prosecutions dragged on for years without final convictions.

title: Revised India-Mauritius Tax Treaty Signed
description: After years of pressure, Mauritius and India signed a protocol in May 2016 amending the 1983 tax treaty to give India source-based taxing rights over capital gains on Indian shares from 2017, with a phased transition to 2019. The change was a major blow to the offshore route but cleared a long-standing irritant in bilateral relations.

title: Pravind Jugnauth Becomes Prime Minister Without Election
description: Aneerood Jugnauth resigned as Prime Minister in January 2017 and arranged for his son Pravind Jugnauth to succeed him without a general election, drawing accusations of dynastic transfer of power. The move was constitutionally permitted but politically controversial and shaped opposition narratives through the 2019 campaign.

title: ICJ Advisory Opinion on Chagos: UK Occupation Unlawful
description: On February 25, 2019, the International Court of Justice issued an advisory opinion finding that the UK's continued administration of the Chagos Archipelago is unlawful and that the decolonisation of Mauritius was not lawfully completed. The UN General Assembly endorsed the opinion 116-6 in May 2019, demanding UK withdrawal within six months — a deadline Britain ignored, but a major diplomatic victory for Mauritius.

title: Pravind Jugnauth's MSM-Lepep Wins November Election
description: Pravind Jugnauth's MSM-led Morisien Alliance won the November 2019 election with 38 seats against the Labour-led National Alliance's 14 and the MMM's 8, securing a full term in his own right. The result confirmed the Jugnauth dynasty's grip on power but was contested in court by the opposition over alleged irregularities.

title: Cyclone Belna Tracks Past Mauritius
description: Tropical Cyclone Belna passed close to Mauritius in December 2019 before making landfall in Madagascar, prompting class-3 warnings and disruption to flights and shipping. While direct damage was limited, the storm formed part of a more active cyclone season highlighting ongoing climate-vulnerability concerns.

title: COVID-19 Lockdown — Tourism Collapse
description: Mauritius confirmed its first COVID-19 cases in March 2020 and imposed one of the world's strictest national lockdowns from March to May, eliminating local transmission until late 2020. Closed borders devastated tourism — typically 8 percent of GDP and a major employer — driving the sharpest GDP contraction since independence (around -15 percent in 2020).

title: Wakashio Oil Spill — Worst Environmental Disaster in Mauritian History
description: The Japanese-owned bulk carrier MV Wakashio ran aground off Pointe d'Esny on July 25, 2020 and began leaking heavy fuel oil on August 6, ultimately spilling about 1,000 tonnes into protected lagoons and mangroves around Blue Bay Marine Park. Volunteer mobilisation was massive but the disaster damaged sensitive ecosystems, killed dozens of dolphins in suspected related strandings, and prompted protests against the government's slow response.

title: FATF Grey-Listing for AML Deficiencies
description: The Financial Action Task Force placed Mauritius on its grey list of jurisdictions with strategic anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorism-financing deficiencies in February 2020, and the EU added Mauritius to its own high-risk list in May 2020. The listings imposed friction on cross-border financial flows and threatened the offshore-finance business model.

title: Mass Protests Over Wakashio and Government Response
description: Tens of thousands marched in Port Louis on August 29, 2020 in the largest demonstration in decades, demanding accountability for the Wakashio response, transparency on the oil-spill investigation, and Pravind Jugnauth's resignation. Further protests followed in September 2020 after the suspicious deaths of activists and a fisherman whose body washed up near the wreck.

title: Vaccination Campaign and Border Reopening
description: Mauritius launched its COVID-19 vaccination programme in early 2021 using donated and procured AstraZeneca, Sinopharm, Covaxin and Pfizer doses, achieving high coverage by year-end. Borders reopened in stages from July to October 2021 with vaccine-passport rules, beginning the tourism recovery.

title: FATF Removes Mauritius from Grey List
description: In October 2021 FATF removed Mauritius from its grey list after the country implemented an action plan strengthening beneficial-ownership transparency, AML supervision, and prosecution capacity. The EU followed with its own removal in early 2022, restoring the country's standing as a financial centre.

title: Tourism Rebounds and GDP Recovery
description: Tourist arrivals rebounded to roughly 80 percent of pre-pandemic levels in 2022, driving an 8.7 percent GDP expansion that recouped most of the COVID contraction. Inflation, however, surged into double digits as global energy and food prices rose with the Ukraine war, eroding household purchasing power.

title: Inflation Crisis and Central Bank Tightening
description: Headline inflation peaked above 11 percent in 2022 amid imported energy and food shocks, prompting the Bank of Mauritius to raise its key rate from 1.85 percent to 4.5 percent in stages. The cost-of-living squeeze became a major political issue and a significant factor in the 2024 election.

title: Moris Lakwizinn Cost-of-Living Movement
description: A series of demonstrations under the 'Moris Lakwizinn' (Mauritius Kitchen) banner from 2022 into 2023 protested rising food and fuel prices, opposition harassment, and corruption scandals. The protests sustained pressure on the Jugnauth government and reinforced opposition narratives ahead of the 2024 election.

title: EU AML Compliance Concerns Resurface
description: Through 2023 and 2024 the EU and several G20 jurisdictions raised renewed concerns about Mauritius's effectiveness in implementing AML standards in practice, despite removal from formal lists. The pressure prompted further legislation on beneficial-ownership registers and corporate-services-provider supervision.

title: UK-Mauritius Chagos Sovereignty Deal Announced
description: On October 3, 2024 the UK and Mauritius announced a political agreement transferring sovereignty of the Chagos Archipelago to Mauritius while leasing Diego Garcia to the UK for an initial 99 years to maintain the joint US-UK military base. The deal was hailed in Port Louis as the culmination of a decades-long campaign but criticised by Chagossian groups excluded from the talks and by sections of the UK opposition.

title: Phone-Tapping Scandal — 'Missie Moustass' Recordings
description: From mid-October 2024, anonymous TikTok account 'Missie Moustass' began publishing leaked recordings of phone calls implicating senior MSM figures, journalists, and businessmen in corruption and political interference. The government's brief social-media blackout in response triggered fierce backlash and dominated the final weeks of the election campaign.

title: Alliance du Changement Landslide Ousts Jugnauth — Ramgoolam Returns
description: In the November 10, 2024 election Navin Ramgoolam's Alliance du Changement (Labour-MMM-ND-RP) won 60 of 62 elected seats against Pravind Jugnauth's Lepep alliance's two, the largest landslide in independent Mauritian history. Ramgoolam, 77, returned as Prime Minister for a third stint, promising anti-corruption reforms and a parliamentary inquiry into the Missie Moustass tapes.

title: Cyclone Belal Causes Flash Flooding in Port Louis
description: Tropical Cyclone Belal struck Mauritius in January 2024, dumping heavy rainfall that triggered flash floods in Port Louis and surrounding areas, killing at least one person and causing extensive infrastructure damage. The disaster exposed urban-drainage weaknesses and prompted criticism of the Meteorological Services for late warnings.

title: Ramgoolam Government Audit Reveals Fiscal Hole
description: Within weeks of taking office, the new Ramgoolam government commissioned an emergency audit that reported a substantially larger fiscal deficit and public-debt burden than previously disclosed by the outgoing administration. The findings were used to justify a contractionary 2025-26 budget including subsidy cuts and tax measures, while triggering accusations of past statistical manipulation.

title: Chagos Treaty Signed and Sent for Ratification
description: Following the October 2024 political agreement, the UK and Mauritius finalised and signed a binding treaty in 2025 transferring Chagos sovereignty to Mauritius and structuring the long-term Diego Garcia base lease, with the agreement subject to parliamentary ratification in both states. The treaty also established a trust fund for Chagossians and infrastructure commitments to the resettled outer islands.

title: Anti-Corruption Inquiries and Asset-Recovery Drive
description: The new Labour-MMM government launched parliamentary commissions of inquiry into the Missie Moustass recordings, MSM-era contract awards, and alleged abuses in the police and intelligence services, alongside an asset-recovery initiative targeting unexplained wealth. Several former officials were charged in 2025, marking the most aggressive accountability push since the Kaya-era inquiries.

title: SAFE Submarine Cable Connects Mauritius to High-Speed International Internet
description: The SAFE (South Africa Far East) submarine fiber-optic cable, a 13,500km system linking South Africa, Mauritius, Reunion, India and Malaysia, entered service in April 2002. The landing gave Mauritius its first high-capacity international broadband connection, with an initial design capacity of 10Gbps later upgraded to 130Gbps, underpinning the island's subsequent growth as a regional data and offshore-services hub.

title: Mauritius Declares State of Environmental Emergency After Oil Spill
description: On August 7, 2020, Mauritius Prime Minister Pravind Jugnauth declared a state of environmental emergency after the Japanese-owned bulk carrier MV Wakashio, which ran aground on a coral reef on July 25, began leaking fuel oil, eventually spilling an estimated 1,000 tonnes near the ecologically sensitive Pointe d'Esny wetlands and Blue Bay Marine Park. The declaration mobilized international assistance and emergency containment measures in what officials called the worst environmental disaster in the country's history. Dozens of dolphins and whales later washed up dead on nearby beaches.
